If it is missing, say so in class, because the gap is probably not only yours.

## B {#sec-glossary-b}

Bayes' theorem
:   The rule that combines prior and likelihood into a posterior.
    Read as a proportionality, the posterior is the likelihood times the prior, up to a constant.

    [The logic of Bayesian inference]{.glossary-tag .glossary-block} [probability]{.glossary-tag}

Branch
:   A named line of development inside a repository, so work in progress does not disturb the main
    version.
    This course uses `main` for sources and `gh-pages` for the rendered website.

    [Scientific programming fundamentals]{.glossary-tag .glossary-block} [git]{.glossary-tag}

`brms`
:   The R package used throughout this course to fit Bayesian regression models with familiar
    formula syntax.
    Every model call here sets its priors explicitly.

    [Applied modelling]{.glossary-tag .glossary-block} [r]{.glossary-tag} [model]{.glossary-tag}


## C {#sec-glossary-c}

Chain
:   One run of the sampler, producing a sequence of draws.
    Several chains are run from different starting points so their agreement can be checked.

    [The logic of Bayesian inference]{.glossary-tag .glossary-block} [mcmc]{.glossary-tag}

Clone
:   Making a local copy of a remote repository, including its history.

    [Scientific programming fundamentals]{.glossary-tag .glossary-block} [git]{.glossary-tag}

Code chunk
:   A block of executable code inside a `.qmd`.
    Every chunk in this course carries a label, so it can be referred to and so an error points
    somewhere specific.

    [Scientific programming fundamentals]{.glossary-tag .glossary-block} [quarto]{.glossary-tag} [r]{.glossary-tag}

Coefficient
:   A parameter multiplying a predictor, describing how the expected outcome changes as that
    predictor changes.
    In a Bayesian model a coefficient has a full posterior, not a single value.

    [Applied modelling]{.glossary-tag .glossary-block} [regression]{.glossary-tag} [interpretation]{.glossary-tag}

Commit
:   One recorded snapshot of the project, with a message saying what changed.
    A commit is the unit of history, so its message is written for the next reader.

    [Scientific programming fundamentals]{.glossary-tag .glossary-block} [git]{.glossary-tag}

Confounder
:   A variable that influences both the presumed cause and the outcome, so leaving it out distorts
    the relationship you are trying to measure.
    Whether a variable is a confounder is a claim about the DAG, not something the data can tell
    you.

    [The logic of Bayesian inference]{.glossary-tag .glossary-block} [model]{.glossary-tag} [interpretation]{.glossary-tag}

Counterfactual prediction
:   A model-based prediction of the outcome under a specified, possibly unobserved, setting of the
    predictors.
    It is how a fitted model answers a substantive question.

    [Applied modelling]{.glossary-tag .glossary-block} [interpretation]{.glossary-tag} [model]{.glossary-tag}

Credible interval
:   A range containing a stated share of the posterior probability, for example 90 percent.
    It is a direct statement about the parameter given the data and the model, which is what makes
    it straightforward to interpret.
    A frequentist confidence interval is a different object, describing the long-run behaviour of
    the procedure rather than the parameter.

    [The logic of Bayesian inference]{.glossary-tag .glossary-block} [interpretation]{.glossary-tag} [probability]{.glossary-tag}


## D {#sec-glossary-d}

Data frame and tibble
:   A rectangular table of data in R, with one column per variable.
    A tibble is the tidyverse version of a data frame, with friendlier printing and fewer
    surprises.

    [Scientific programming fundamentals]{.glossary-tag .glossary-block} [data]{.glossary-tag} [r]{.glossary-tag}

Directed acyclic graph
:   A diagram of assumed causal relationships, drawn as arrows between variables with no cycles.
    Usually called a DAG, it makes explicit which variables must be adjusted for and which must
    not.

    [The logic of Bayesian inference]{.glossary-tag .glossary-block} [workflow]{.glossary-tag} [model]{.glossary-tag}

Divergent transition
:   A warning that the sampler failed to explore part of the posterior faithfully.
    Divergences are not cosmetic, so they are understood rather than silenced.

    [The logic of Bayesian inference]{.glossary-tag .glossary-block} [mcmc]{.glossary-tag} [diagnostics]{.glossary-tag}

Draw
:   A single sample from the posterior.
    A posterior is represented in practice as a large collection of draws, and every summary is
    computed from them.

    [The logic of Bayesian inference]{.glossary-tag .glossary-block} [mcmc]{.glossary-tag}


## E {#sec-glossary-e}

Effective sample size
:   How many independent draws the correlated MCMC draws are worth.
    A low value means a summary rests on less information than the raw number of draws suggests.

    [The logic of Bayesian inference]{.glossary-tag .glossary-block} [mcmc]{.glossary-tag} [diagnostics]{.glossary-tag}

Estimand
:   The quantity you actually want to know, stated precisely, before any model is fitted.
    Naming it first is step 1 of the workflow, and it is what keeps a model answerable to a
    question.

    [The logic of Bayesian inference]{.glossary-tag .glossary-block} [workflow]{.glossary-tag} [interpretation]{.glossary-tag}


## F {#sec-glossary-f}

Freeze
:   Quarto's cache of already-computed results, stored in `_freeze/`, so a rebuild does not re-run
    expensive code.
    It is committed deliberately, so the site rebuilds identically anywhere.

    [Scientific programming fundamentals]{.glossary-tag .glossary-block} [quarto]{.glossary-tag} [workflow]{.glossary-tag}

Function and argument
:   A function is a named, reusable piece of code, and its arguments are the inputs you give it.
    Naming arguments explicitly makes code readable a month later.

    [Scientific programming fundamentals]{.glossary-tag .glossary-block} [r]{.glossary-tag}


## G {#sec-glossary-g}

Generative model
:   A model complete enough to simulate fake data that looks like the real thing.
    If you can simulate from it, you can check it before it ever touches your data.

    [The logic of Bayesian inference]{.glossary-tag .glossary-block} [model]{.glossary-tag}

Git
:   A version control system that records the history of a project as a series of snapshots.
    It answers what changed, when, and why, and it lets you go back.

    [Scientific programming fundamentals]{.glossary-tag .glossary-block} [git]{.glossary-tag}

GitHub
:   The platform that hosts repositories and adds collaboration features such as issues and
    automated checks.
    Course materials are distributed and homework submitted through it.

    [Scientific programming fundamentals]{.glossary-tag .glossary-block} [git]{.glossary-tag}


## H {#sec-glossary-h}

`here()`
:   The function from the `here` package that builds a path from the project root rather than from
    whatever the current working directory happens to be.
    Use it for every path, always.

    [Scientific programming fundamentals]{.glossary-tag .glossary-block} [r]{.glossary-tag} [workflow]{.glossary-tag}


## I {#sec-glossary-i}

Interaction
:   A term letting the effect of one predictor depend on the value of another.
    An interaction is a claim that an effect is conditional, so it is interpreted jointly and not
    term by term.

    [Applied modelling]{.glossary-tag .glossary-block} [regression]{.glossary-tag} [interpretation]{.glossary-tag}

Intercept
:   The expected outcome when every predictor is zero.
    It is only interpretable when zero is a meaningful value, which is one reason predictors are
    often centred.

    [Applied modelling]{.glossary-tag .glossary-block} [regression]{.glossary-tag} [interpretation]{.glossary-tag}


## L {#sec-glossary-l}

Likelihood
:   How probable the observed data would be, for each candidate value of the parameters.
    It is the part of the model that lets the data speak.

    [The logic of Bayesian inference]{.glossary-tag .glossary-block} [probability]{.glossary-tag} [model]{.glossary-tag}

Linear regression
:   A model in which the expected outcome is a straight-line function of the predictors.
    The foundation the later models extend rather than replace.

    [Applied modelling]{.glossary-tag .glossary-block} [regression]{.glossary-tag}

Link function
:   The transformation connecting a linear predictor to the scale of the outcome.
    It lets a linear model describe outcomes that are bounded, such as probabilities.

    [Applied modelling]{.glossary-tag .glossary-block} [regression]{.glossary-tag} [model]{.glossary-tag}

Literate programming
:   Writing code and the prose that explains it in a single document, so the reasoning and the
    computation cannot drift apart.
    Quarto is the tool we use for it.

    [Scientific programming fundamentals]{.glossary-tag .glossary-block} [workflow]{.glossary-tag} [quarto]{.glossary-tag}

Log-odds
:   The scale a logistic regression's coefficients live on, the logarithm of the odds.
    Coefficients are additive here but not on the probability scale, which is why results are
    converted before interpretation.

    [Applied modelling]{.glossary-tag .glossary-block} [regression]{.glossary-tag} [interpretation]{.glossary-tag}

Logistic regression
:   A model for a binary outcome, using the logit link to keep predicted probabilities between zero
    and one.

    [Applied modelling]{.glossary-tag .glossary-block} [regression]{.glossary-tag}


## M {#sec-glossary-m}

Marginal effect
:   How the expected outcome changes with a predictor, after averaging over the others.
    It is often the form in which a result becomes reportable.

    [Applied modelling]{.glossary-tag .glossary-block} [interpretation]{.glossary-tag}

Markov chain Monte Carlo
:   A family of algorithms, usually shortened to MCMC, that explore the posterior by taking a long,
    dependent random walk through it.
    We need it because most interesting posteriors cannot be written down in closed form.

    [The logic of Bayesian inference]{.glossary-tag .glossary-block} [mcmc]{.glossary-tag}

Multilevel model
:   A model with parameters that vary by group, where the group-level variation is itself
    estimated.
    Also called a hierarchical model.

    [Applied modelling]{.glossary-tag .glossary-block} [multilevel]{.glossary-tag}


## N {#sec-glossary-n}

Native pipe
:   The `|>` operator, which passes the result on its left into the first argument of the function
    on its right, so a sequence of steps reads left to right.
    This course uses `|>` throughout and not the older `%>%`.

    [Scientific programming fundamentals]{.glossary-tag .glossary-block} [r]{.glossary-tag}

Normalising constant
:   The quantity that rescales the posterior so it integrates to one.
    It does not depend on the parameters, which is why we can usually ignore it and work with the
    unnormalised posterior.

    [The logic of Bayesian inference]{.glossary-tag .glossary-block} [probability]{.glossary-tag}


## P {#sec-glossary-p}

Package
:   A bundle of functions, data and documentation that extends R.
    Installed once with `install.packages()`, loaded per session with `library()`.

    [Scientific programming fundamentals]{.glossary-tag .glossary-block} [r]{.glossary-tag}

Parameter
:   An unknown quantity in a model that we want to learn about, such as a slope or an average.
    Bayesian inference gives a parameter a distribution rather than one fixed number.

    [The logic of Bayesian inference]{.glossary-tag .glossary-block} [probability]{.glossary-tag} [model]{.glossary-tag}

Partial pooling
:   The compromise a multilevel model strikes between one estimate for all groups and a separate,
    independent estimate per group.
    Groups with little data are pulled towards the overall pattern, and groups with plenty are left
    largely alone.

    [Applied modelling]{.glossary-tag .glossary-block} [multilevel]{.glossary-tag}

Population-level and group-level effects
:   Population-level effects apply across all observations, and group-level effects vary by group.
    `brms` uses these names for what are elsewhere called fixed and random effects.

    [Applied modelling]{.glossary-tag .glossary-block} [multilevel]{.glossary-tag} [model]{.glossary-tag}

Posterior
:   The distribution of the parameters after conditioning on the data.
    This is what Bayes' theorem returns, and every quantity of interest is computed from it.

    [The logic of Bayesian inference]{.glossary-tag .glossary-block} [probability]{.glossary-tag} [model]{.glossary-tag}

Posterior predictive check
:   Simulating data from the fitted model and comparing it against the observed data.
    It asks whether the model can reproduce the features of the data you care about.

    [The logic of Bayesian inference]{.glossary-tag .glossary-block} [diagnostics]{.glossary-tag} [model]{.glossary-tag}

Posterior predictive distribution
:   The distribution of new outcomes implied by the fitted model, accounting for both parameter
    uncertainty and outcome variability.
    Predictions come from it rather than from point estimates alone.

    [Applied modelling]{.glossary-tag .glossary-block} [interpretation]{.glossary-tag} [model]{.glossary-tag}

Prior
:   The distribution expressing what is plausible about a parameter before seeing the data.
    A prior is a philosophical commitment, so it is defended on principled grounds rather than
    chosen for convenience.

    [The logic of Bayesian inference]{.glossary-tag .glossary-block} [prior]{.glossary-tag} [model]{.glossary-tag}

Prior predictive check
:   Simulating data from the priors alone, before fitting, to see what outcomes the model considers
    plausible.
    It catches priors that imply impossible values, such as a turnout rate above 100 percent.

    [The logic of Bayesian inference]{.glossary-tag .glossary-block} [prior]{.glossary-tag} [diagnostics]{.glossary-tag}

Probability distribution
:   A description of how plausible each possible value of a quantity is.
    Here, distributions describe both data and parameters, which is the central move of the
    Bayesian approach.

    [The logic of Bayesian inference]{.glossary-tag .glossary-block} [probability]{.glossary-tag}

Project root
:   The top directory of a project, the fixed point every other path is expressed relative to.
    Anchoring paths to it is what makes a project work on a machine other than yours.

    [Scientific programming fundamentals]{.glossary-tag .glossary-block} [workflow]{.glossary-tag} [r]{.glossary-tag}

Push and pull
:   Sending your local commits to the remote (push), and fetching other people's commits from it
    (pull).

    [Scientific programming fundamentals]{.glossary-tag .glossary-block} [git]{.glossary-tag}


## Q {#sec-glossary-q}

Quantity of interest
:   The specific, interpretable number a reader should take away, computed from the posterior.
    Deciding it in advance is what stops an analysis becoming a table of coefficients with no
    conclusion.

    [Applied modelling]{.glossary-tag .glossary-block} [interpretation]{.glossary-tag}

Quarto
:   The publishing system that turns a `.qmd` file into HTML, PDF or slides, running the embedded
    code as it goes.
    Everything in this course, including this page, is a Quarto document.

    [Scientific programming fundamentals]{.glossary-tag .glossary-block} [quarto]{.glossary-tag}


## R {#sec-glossary-r}

R-hat
:   A convergence diagnostic comparing variation between chains against variation within them.
    Values near 1 are consistent with convergence, and clearly larger values mean the chains do
    not agree.

    [The logic of Bayesian inference]{.glossary-tag .glossary-block} [mcmc]{.glossary-tag} [diagnostics]{.glossary-tag}

Remote
:   A copy of the repository hosted elsewhere, normally on GitHub, that you push to and pull from.
    The remote is what makes the work shared rather than local.

    [Scientific programming fundamentals]{.glossary-tag .glossary-block} [git]{.glossary-tag}

Render
:   The act of turning a source `.qmd` into its output document.
    A submission that does not render is not a submission, because nobody else can reproduce it.

    [Scientific programming fundamentals]{.glossary-tag .glossary-block} [quarto]{.glossary-tag} [workflow]{.glossary-tag}

Repository
:   A project under version control, together with its full history.
    Usually shortened to "repo".

    [Scientific programming fundamentals]{.glossary-tag .glossary-block} [git]{.glossary-tag}

Reproducible research
:   Research whose results can be regenerated from the raw data and the code alone, by someone
    else, on another machine.
    The practical test is whether one command rebuilds every number and figure in the output.

    [Scientific programming fundamentals]{.glossary-tag .glossary-block} [workflow]{.glossary-tag}


## S {#sec-glossary-s}

`set.seed()`
:   Fixes the starting point of R's random number generator, so anything involving randomness
    gives the same result on every run.
    Required wherever this course simulates or samples.

    [Scientific programming fundamentals]{.glossary-tag .glossary-block} [r]{.glossary-tag} [workflow]{.glossary-tag}

Shrinkage
:   The pull of a group's estimate towards the overall mean under partial pooling.
    It is a feature, because it stops small groups producing extreme estimates on thin evidence.

    [Applied modelling]{.glossary-tag .glossary-block} [multilevel]{.glossary-tag}

Stan
:   The probabilistic programming language and sampler that `brms` compiles models down to and
    runs.
    You will rarely write Stan code directly, but its diagnostics are the ones you read.

    [Applied modelling]{.glossary-tag .glossary-block} [mcmc]{.glossary-tag} [model]{.glossary-tag}


## T {#sec-glossary-t}

Template repository
:   A repository GitHub can copy to make a fresh, independent repository with no shared history.
    Every homework starter is distributed this way, which is why your submission repo is yours
    alone.

    [Scientific programming fundamentals]{.glossary-tag .glossary-block} [git]{.glossary-tag}

Tidy data
:   Data arranged so that each variable is a column, each observation is a row, and each cell holds
    one value.
    Most of the work in an analysis is getting data into this shape, and most tools assume it.

    [Scientific programming fundamentals]{.glossary-tag .glossary-block} [data]{.glossary-tag}

Trace plot
:   A plot of drawn values against iteration, one line per chain.
    Well-mixed chains overlap and look stationary, like noise around a stable level.

    [The logic of Bayesian inference]{.glossary-tag .glossary-block} [mcmc]{.glossary-tag} [diagnostics]{.glossary-tag}


## W {#sec-glossary-w}

Warmup
:   The initial draws a chain uses to adapt and find the posterior, discarded before inference.
    They describe the sampler getting started, not the posterior.

    [The logic of Bayesian inference]{.glossary-tag .glossary-block} [mcmc]{.glossary-tag}

Working directory
:   The directory R currently treats as "here" when it resolves a relative path.
    It changes depending on how code is run, which is exactly why we do not rely on it.

    [Scientific programming fundamentals]{.glossary-tag .glossary-block} [r]{.glossary-tag} [workflow]{.glossary-tag}


## Y {#sec-glossary-y}

YAML front matter
:   The block between the two `---` lines at the top of a `.qmd`, which sets the document title,
    output format and options.
    It is configuration, not content.

    [Scientific programming fundamentals]{.glossary-tag .glossary-block} [quarto]{.glossary-tag}
